In 2008, Elon Musk faced a decision that would have broken most people

Two companies he had poured his heart, soul, and everything he had into were on the brink of collapse. He had just $30 to $40 million left, and saving one meant risking the life of the other

He was forced to confront an almost impossible question: Which of the two dreams he had sacrificed so much to build was he willing to let die?

His answer was neither

Even if it meant risking everything he had left

Tesla and SpaceX were both fighting for survival, and he had to make one of the hardest choices of his life

"I had two choices. I could put it all into one company, and then the other company would definitely die. Or split it between the two companies. But if I split it between the two companies, then both might die"

Then Elon said something that tells you everything about how much these companies meant to him:

"When you put your blood, sweat, and tears into creating something or building something, it's like a child. And so it's like which one am I gonna let starve to death? I couldn't bring myself to do it"

He split the money between both companies, knowing he was risking losing everything

"Fortunately, thank goodness, they both came through"

Nearly two decades later, Tesla has transformed the electric vehicle industry, and SpaceX has revolutionized spaceflight

Two companies that were on the brink of collapse went on to change the world

All because Elon Musk couldn't bring himself to let either one starve

NEW UNDERCOVER INVESTIGATION: I spent several months investigating a nationwide network of advocacy organizations and medical providers helping families continue medically transitioning their children in defiance of state laws.

My investigation centers on Campaign for Southern Equality (CSE), an LGBT advocacy nonprofit that connects families with cooperating medical providers across the country. CSE has distributed over $1 million in travel grants to more than 1,200 families, plus another $1 million to partner organizations, including funding for medical appointments.

With CSE's knowledge, providers in its referral network told me the ways that they circumvent state restrictions on gender-transition treatments for minors.

Some discussed using alternative diagnosis codes, such as “endocrine disorder,” to facilitate prescriptions or insurance coverage. Others described mailing medications directly to families' homes or sending prescriptions to pharmacies in states where these interventions are banned.

Providers also discussed conducting virtual appointments with patients in those states. Others required patients to cross state lines for telehealth but did not appear to have a reliable method for verifying their physical location.

My primary undercover scenario involved an 11-year-old girl in Tennessee who had only recently begun identifying as nonbinary, with no long history of gender-related distress. The providers I shared this scenario with seemed eager to treat her. Many indicated that puberty blockers could be prescribed after an initial evaluation lasting just one to several hours.

My investigation uncovered practices that may violate state and federal laws and pose medical risks to children living hundreds or thousands of miles from their treating physicians.

Read my full @CityJournal investigation: https://t.co/pUesvsGHHo

Anthropic has filed for a record $2 trillion IPO. In a talk uploaded November 30, 2025, a stockbroker asked Elon Musk which company he would buy. Musk said he has no portfolio, then named Google and Nvidia.

The man asking is Nikhil Kamath, who told Musk his primary job is stockbroker and stock investor. Musk runs Tesla, SpaceX, xAI and X, and says the output of AI and robotics "will dwarf everything else."

The clip is three moments from a 114-minute conversation. The full talk is free on YouTube. In it Musk says US deficits run on the order of $2 trillion a year, and that interest payments on the debt exceed the entire US military budget.

His rules for money fit on a napkin.

Judge the product, not the price. His test for any stock: do you like what the company makes, do you like the roadmap, do you believe in the team. A company, he says, is a group of people assembled to make products and services.

Expect the swings. That test does not solve for daily moves, which he admits are sometimes pretty extreme. His advice is to hold and not worry about them.

Watch the ratio. Inflation, he says, is goods and services output against growth in the money supply. AI has not yet raised output enough. He guesses output growth passes money growth in about three years.

Know the fix on offer. He says the only thing that can solve the US debt is AI and robotics. That is a bet, and he says so.

Money is a tool. He calls it an information system for labor allocation. A trillion dollars on a desert island buys nothing, because there is no labor to allocate.

Check who owns it. When he says AI, robotics and maybe spaceflight will hold almost all the value, he runs companies in each of those fields.

"I don't look for things to invest in. I just try to build things."

Listen from 86:12.

Before you buy into any IPO this month, write down what the company sells, what it ships next and who builds it. If you cannot fill in all three lines, you are not investing. You are buying a headline with your name on it.

I am speechless. Thomas Aquinas College just dropped a study on the rigor of the new SAT.

It compares the 1980/87 test with 2026. The findings should terrify every parent and teacher...

Vocabulary has collapsed.

Old SAT: 70.6% of questions tested vocab.
New SAT: 15%.

The old test forced students to know a wide range of words through analogies, antonyms, and sentence completions. The new test abandoned that. Most vocab questions now just ask students to fill in one blank from context.

Reading passages also got radically shorter (average ~97 words vs 300–340).

The new test uses short expository passages and hands you the necessary background knowledge inside the text. The older tests leaned much more heavily on argumentative and persuasive writing, assumed far more historical, scientific, and cultural knowledge, and penalized students who lacked it.

This is a redefinition of what "college readiness" means.

If you believe that kids should develop rigorous vocabulary, be capable of sustained reading, and possess background knowledge, I have bad news for you. The SAT no longer measures these.

If you want a future where children can actually read difficult texts and construct complex arguments, the SAT must be replaced now.

This cannot go on.
